headline: 9 LLM Evaluation Metrics: Production Architecture Pattern
summary: Most teams evaluate LLMs with a single metric, missing critical failures. This carousel reveals the multi-signal evaluation architecture used by top teams to catch regressions before users do.

slides.title: Why LLM Evaluation Breaks in Production
slides.subtitle: Single metrics miss critical failure modes that only appear at scale
slides.body: Teams ship models that pass benchmarks but fail users. The gap? Evaluation that doesn't mirror real-world complexity.
slides.deep_dive: In development, a single accuracy score feels sufficient. But production reveals edge cases, distribution shifts, and adversarial inputs that no single metric captures. This carousel reveals the evaluation architecture pattern that separates toy demos from reliable systems.
slides.key_fact: No single metric correlates with human preference across all tasks
slides.why_it_matters: Prevents silent model degradation and costly rollbacks

slides.title: Evaluation as a Diagnostic Panel, Not a Thermometer
slides.subtitle: Like a doctor ordering multiple tests, not just checking temperature
slides.body: A thermometer gives one number. A diagnostic panel runs blood work, imaging, vitals for a complete picture. LLM evaluation needs this multi-signal approach.
slides.deep_dive: Each metric measures a different dimension: factuality, coherence, safety, style, reasoning. Just as a doctor wouldn't diagnose from temperature alone, engineers shouldn't deploy from one score alone. The mental model shifts from 'what's the score?' to 'what does each signal tell us about system health?'
slides.key_fact: 9 distinct metric categories cover orthogonal quality dimensions
slides.why_it_matters: Prevents blind spots where models optimize one metric while degrading others

steps.title: Identify Risk Dimensions
steps.desc: Map product risks to quality categories (factuality, safety, style, etc.)

steps.title: Select Metric Per Dimension
steps.desc: Choose best proxy for each risk — reference-based, reference-free, or LLM-judge

steps.title: Set Guardrail Thresholds
steps.desc: Define non-regression floors, not just improvement targets

steps.title: Monitor Correlations
steps.desc: Weekly review to detect Goodhart's Law — when metric improves but quality drops

slides.title: From Model Output to Actionable Signal
slides.subtitle: Input → Metric Computation → Aggregated Dashboard → Alert Threshold
slides.body: Raw generations flow through parallel metric pipelines. Each computes a score. Aggregation layers combine signals. Thresholds trigger human review or rollback.
slides.deep_dive: The execution path: 1) Sample model outputs stratified by task type. 2) Run each through reference-based metrics (needs ground truth), reference-free metrics (quality proxies), and LLM-as-judge evaluators. 3) Normalize scores to common scale. 4) Weight by business criticality. 5) Dashboard with trend lines and anomaly detection. 6) Automated alerts when composite score drops or any critical metric regresses.
slides.key_fact: Parallel metric computation adds latency but enables comprehensive coverage
slides.why_it_matters: Enables continuous evaluation without blocking inference pipeline
slides.input: Model outputs + ground truth (when available) + task metadata
slides.processing: Parallel pipelines: reference-based metrics, reference-free metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluators → normalization → weighted aggregation
slides.output: Per-metric scores, composite health index, trend lines, regression alerts

slides.title: The Evaluation Triangle: Speed, Cost, Depth
slides.subtitle: Pick two: fast automated metrics, cheap human eval, or deep semantic understanding
slides.body: Automated metrics run in milliseconds but miss nuance. Human eval captures nuance but costs dollars per sample. LLM-as-judge sits in the middle.
slides.deep_dive: Architectural trade-offs: Reference-based metrics need ground truth — impossible for open-ended tasks. Reference-free metrics scale but correlate weakly with human judgment. LLM-as-judge offers semantic depth at 100x human cost reduction but introduces evaluator bias. Production systems layer all three: automated metrics on 100% of traffic, LLM-as-judge on 1-5% sample, human eval on critical failures only.
slides.key_fact: Layered evaluation reduces cost 100x vs full human eval while catching 90% of critical issues
slides.why_it_matters: Directly impacts inference latency budget and operational expenditure

slides.title: Single-Metric Tunnel Vision vs Multi-Signal Dashboard
slides.subtitle: Optimizing one metric while toxicity spikes is a production disaster waiting to happen
slides.body: ❌ Naive: Track one headline metric, celebrate when it improves. ✅ Robust: Monitor 9-metric dashboard with correlation analysis and regression alerts.
slides.deep_dive: The antipattern: Teams pick one metric (often BLEU or accuracy) because it's familiar. They optimize prompts, fine-tuning, and RAG pipelines for that metric. Meanwhile, factuality drops, verbosity explodes, or safety violations increase — all invisible to the single metric. The robust pattern: Define a metric portfolio covering accuracy, safety, style, latency, cost. Set guardrails for each. Alert on any metric crossing threshold. Weekly review metric correlations to detect Goodhart's Law in action.
slides.key_fact: Single-metric optimization routinely degrades unmeasured dimensions
slides.why_it_matters: Prevents 'metric gaming' where models improve scores but worsen user experience

slides.title: How Top Teams Run Continuous Evaluation at Millions of Requests/Day
slides.subtitle: Sampling, shadow evaluation, and automated regression gates
slides.body: They don't evaluate every request. They stratify sample, run shadow pipelines, and gate deployments behind metric thresholds.
slides.deep_dive: Production pattern: 1) Stratified sampling by task type, user tier, language. 2) Shadow evaluation: new model runs alongside production, outputs logged but not served. 3) Automated metric suite runs on shadow outputs. 4) Statistical significance testing against production baseline. 5) Deployment gate: all critical metrics must be non-inferior (p<0.05). 6) Canary rollout with real-time metric monitoring. 7) Automated rollback if any metric regresses beyond threshold. This pattern enables daily model updates with near-zero risk.
slides.key_fact: Shadow evaluation + statistical gating enables safe daily model deployments
slides.why_it_matters: Turns evaluation from a bottleneck into a continuous deployment enabler

slides.title: Build Your Evaluation Architecture in 3 Steps
slides.subtitle: Start with critical metrics, layer automation, gate deployments
slides.body: 1) Define 3-5 guardrail metrics for your use case. 2) Automate computation in shadow pipeline. 3) Block deployments on regression.
slides.deep_dive: Actionable framework: Step 1 — Map your product risks to metric categories (factuality for RAG, safety for chat, style for creative). Pick 3-5 non-negotiable guardrails. Step 2 — Build shadow evaluation pipeline: sample 1% of traffic, run full metric suite, store results with metadata. Step 3 — Implement deployment gates: CI/CD fails if any guardrail metric shows statistically significant regression. Bonus: Weekly metric correlation review to detect emerging blind spots. This transforms evaluation from academic exercise to engineering safety net.
slides.key_fact: Guardrail metrics + shadow pipeline + deployment gates = production-grade evaluation
slides.why_it_matters: Catches regressions before users do, enables confident iteration
takeaways: Define 3-5 guardrail metrics tied to product risks
Build shadow evaluation pipeline with stratified sampling

slides.title: 9-Metric Portfolio Checklist
slides.subtitle: Verify your evaluation covers all critical dimensions
slides.body: Use this checklist to audit your evaluation coverage before next release.
slides.deep_dive: A complete evaluation portfolio spans: 1) Reference-based accuracy (needs ground truth). 2) Reference-free fluency (perplexity, learned quality). 3) Semantic similarity (embedding-based). 4) Factuality/grounding (for RAG). 5) Safety/toxicity (classifier-based). 6) Instruction following (LLM-as-judge). 7) Reasoning quality (step-by-step verification). 8) Style/tone adherence (classifier or LLM-judge). 9) Latency/cost efficiency (system metrics). Missing any category? That's a blind spot. Prioritize based on product risk profile.
slides.key_fact: 9 categories map to distinct failure modes — gaps equal production risk
slides.why_it_matters: Ensures no critical quality dimension goes unmeasured
